title: Josaphat (12 November)
hook: a Ukrainian Greek Catholic archbishop killed in the struggles over unity

segments.voice: Last time, Simon and Jude, two apostles the Gospels barely mention. Your line was the forgotten apostles. Whose name did you say kindly? Day one thousand forty.

On the night before he dies, in John's Gospel, Jesus prays out loud for his friends. Then he widens the prayer to people who will believe later, people he will never meet in the flesh. And he asks one thing for all of them: "That they all may be one." Christians have carried that line for a long time, and they have not always kept it. Sometimes the arguments over what unity means have been fierce. Today's saint lived inside one of those arguments, and it cost him his life. Today's word is a monk from the lands of Ukraine and Belarus who became an archbishop.
screen: `A PRAYER ON THE LAST NIGHT.` → `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.` → `A LINE NOT ALWAYS KEPT.`

segments.voice: Josaphat grew up in the Eastern Christian world, the world of icons, of the Byzantine liturgy sung in Church Slavonic, of married parish priests and long fasts. In his time some bishops of that church entered into union with the bishop of Rome. They kept their own liturgy, their own customs, their own way of praying, and they accepted the pope's authority. Others refused, and stayed with the Orthodox Church. Families, towns and parishes were split. Josaphat became a monk, then archbishop of Polotsk, on the side of the union. He preached, he cared for the poor, and he worked hard to bring people into the union he believed in. Here's the honest part. The struggle was bitter, and historians record harsh pressure and anger on more than one side. Josaphat was killed by a crowd in a town of his diocese, by people opposed to the union. The Catholic Church honors him as a martyr. Orthodox Christians remember those same years with their own wounds, and the two churches still tell that history differently. That's why his feast can be a hard one, and why the practice today isn't about winning. Today Catholic and Orthodox Christians meet, talk and sometimes pray together. The Eastern Catholic churches, like the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church that especially honors Josaphat, hold together two things: an Eastern way of worship and communion with Rome. His life asks what unity costs, and who pays it.
screen: `AN EASTERN CHRISTIAN WORLD.` · `UNION WITH ROME, AND A SPLIT.` · `KILLED IN THE STRUGGLE.` · `REMEMBERED DIFFERENTLY BY TWO CHURCHES.` · then, large: `DIED FOR UNITY.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: hold Christian unity in mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind Christians who are not like each other: a Catholic parish, an Orthodox church with its icons, a Protestant congregation down the road. Pick the one you know least, and name one thing its people love: a hymn, a fast, a way of reading the Bible, a saint. Let that one thing stand on its own, with no comparison. If you pray, you can pray the line from John's Gospel, that they all may be one. If you don't, simply wish that community well for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Josaphat. An Eastern Catholic monk and archbishop of Polotsk, killed in the struggle over union with Rome, and honored by the Catholic Church as a martyr.
Your line: died for unity. Today, in one disagreement, look for the thing you and the other person share before you speak. Day one thousand forty.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Josaphat on 12 November; Ukrainian Greek Catholics and other Eastern Catholics honor him with particular devotion, and Catholics often pray for Christian unity on his feast.

fork.setup: you're a Christian in Josaphat's lands, and your town is split over union with Rome. a neighbor on the other side is in need. what do you do?
options: ignore them until they change sides.
fork.reveal: there's no single answer in the record for neighbors; the record shows how bitter the split became, and both churches still carry it.

notes: Audit (2026-10-01): practice rewritten; it repeated day 1029's 'bring to mind a split family, don't take a side, hold both' almost exactly. Fork reveal no longer points at the old practice.

Sensitive day: the script tries to describe the Union of Brest era fairly, naming harsh pressure 'on more than one side' and saying Catholics and Orthodox remember it differently. A Catholic Keeper and, ideally, an Eastern Catholic reader should check that this neither blames Orthodox Christians nor diminishes the Church's honoring of Josaphat as a martyr.

Facts to confirm: Josaphat as a Basilian monk, archbishop of Polotsk, killed by a crowd opposed to the union in a town of his diocese (Vitebsk). No dates, numbers or the name of the town are given in the voice.
Original: Ukrainian 'Йосафат' and the note that the name recalls a king of Judah (Jehoshaphat); confirm spelling and pronunciation.
